questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. The ulcer has a clean base, indurated edges, and is associated with non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy of the lesion exudate shows motile spiral organisms. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: The classic triad of a painless, indurated ulcer with clean base (Hunterian chancre), non-tender lymphadenopathy, and motile spirochetes on dark-field microscopy is diagnostic of primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Haemophilus ducreyi causes painful chancroid. Chlamydia trachomatis causes lymphogranuloma venereum. Klebsiella granulomatis causes donovanosis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with SLE presents with tense bullae on sun-exposed areas, oral ulcers, and a positive Nikolsky sign. Histopathology shows subepidermal blister with neutrophilic infiltrate. Direct immunofluorescence reveals linear IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous SLE presents in SLE patients with tense subepidermal bullae on sun-exposed areas and linear IgA deposits at the DEJ on DIF. It is distinguished from linear IgA bullous dermatosis by the underlying SLE and clinical context. BP shows linear IgG/C3. EBA shows IgG targeting type VII collagen. The neutrophilic infiltrate and SLE background clinch the diagnosis of bullous SLE.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a chronic verrucous plaque on the foot with black dots on the surface. He reports a thorn prick injury 6 months ago. KOH mount reveals thick-walled, septate, copper-colored round cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents as verrucous plaques with black dots (transepidermal elimination of fungal elements) after traumatic inoculation. KOH shows pathognomonic sclerotic bodies (Medlar bodies / copper pennies) — thick-walled, brown, septate, muriform cells. Mycetoma shows grains in sinuses. Sporotrichosis shows lymphocutaneous spread. Phaeohyphomycosis shows hyphae, not sclerotic bodies.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with overlying telangiectasias on the nose that has been slowly growing for 2 years. Dermoscopy reveals arborizing vessels and spoke-wheel areas. What is the treatment of choice for this lesion located in the nasal H-zone?
opts: Wide local excision with 1 cm margin
questions.exp: For basal cell carcinoma (BCC) in high-risk areas like the nose (H-zone of the face), Mohs micrographic surgery is the treatment of choice due to superior margin control and tissue conservation. Standard excision with 1 cm margin is for melanoma. Topical treatments are only for superficial BCC. Arborizing vessels and spoke-wheel areas on dermoscopy are pathognomonic for BCC.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man with borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy on 6 months of multidrug therapy suddenly develops erythema and tenderness over existing skin lesions along with fever and acute nerve pain. Slit skin smear is negative. What is the best management?
questions.exp: Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) occurs in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL) as a delayed-type hypersensitivity response. It presents with swelling and erythema of existing patches and acute neuritis. Treatment is prednisolone starting at 40 mg/day and tapering over 6 months while continuing MDT. Type 2 (ENL) occurs in lepromatous leprosy and is treated with thalidomide or clofazimine.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, arthralgia, and hair loss. ANA is positive (1:640, homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA antibodies are elevated. Which complement component deficiency is most strongly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: C1q deficiency is the single strongest genetic risk factor for SLE. C1q normally helps clear apoptotic debris; its deficiency leads to accumulation of nuclear antigens, driving autoantibody production. Over 90% of individuals with complete C1q deficiency develop a lupus-like syndrome. C2 and C4 deficiencies are also associated but less strongly. Properdin deficiency predisposes to Neisseria infections.

questions.q: A 40-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 80 cells/µL) presents with extensive molluscum contagiosum with giant lesions (>1 cm) on the face. He is started on antiretroviral therapy. What is the expected course of the molluscum after ART initiation?
opts: Rapid worsening due to immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome
Gradual resolution as CD4 count recovers
No change; molluscum requires specific antiviral treatment
questions.exp: In HIV patients, molluscum contagiosum tends to be extensive and giant when CD4 is low. With ART, as CD4 count recovers, the immune system can clear MCV, and lesions gradually resolve. IRIS can cause transient worsening of some infections but molluscum typically improves. Molluscum does not transform to KS (KS is caused by HHV-8). Specific antiviral therapy is not routinely required if immune recovery occurs.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with painful grouped vesicles along the right T4 dermatome. He develops severe burning pain that persists 4 months after the rash heals. What is the most effective prevention strategy for this complication?
opts: Early antiviral therapy with acyclovir within 72 hours of rash onset
Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) given before disease onset
Topical lidocaine patch applied to the acute lesions
questions.exp: The recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix, RZV) given before disease onset reduces the risk of herpes zoster by ~97% and postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) by ~91% in adults ≥50 years. Early antivirals reduce severity of acute disease and may modestly reduce PHN risk but are not as effective for prevention as vaccination. Gabapentin and lidocaine treat established PHN.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with white, curdy vaginal discharge with severe pruritus. KOH mount shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast cells. She has been on broad-spectrum antibiotics for 2 weeks. What is the drug of choice for treatment?
opts: Oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 7 days
Single oral dose of fluconazole 150 mg
Oral itraconazole 200 mg BD for 1 day
questions.exp: Vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by Candida albicans (pseudohyphae + budding yeast on KOH) after antibiotic use is most conveniently treated with a single oral dose of fluconazole 150 mg, which is equally effective to topical azoles and preferred for patient compliance. Topical clotrimazole is an alternative but requires longer treatment. Metronidazole treats bacterial vaginosis/trichomoniasis.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth that started as vesicles. Gram stain of the exudate shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the first-line topical treatment?
questions.exp: Impetigo caused by Staphylococcus aureus presenting as honey-colored crusted lesions in a child is best treated topically with mupirocin 2% ointment. Mupirocin inhibits bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase and is highly effective against S. aureus including MRSA. Fusidic acid is an alternative in some regions. Oral antibiotics are used for extensive disease. Neomycin has less efficacy and higher sensitization risk.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with silvery-white scales over erythematous plaques on the elbows, knees, and scalp, with nail pitting and joint pain. Auspitz sign is positive. Which cytokine pathway is the primary target of the most effective biologic therapies for this condition?
questions.exp: Psoriasis pathogenesis centers on the IL-23/Th17/IL-17 axis. IL-23 drives differentiation of Th17 cells, which produce IL-17A, the primary effector cytokine causing keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Biologics targeting this pathway (anti-IL-17: secukinumab, ixekizumab; anti-IL-23 p19: guselkumab, risankizumab) show superior efficacy over older TNF-α inhibitors. IL-4/IL-13 is targeted in atopic dermatitis (dupilumab).

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with hypopigmented, anesthetic patches on the trunk. Slit skin smear bacteriological index (BI) is 0. Histopathology shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells and lymphocytic infiltrate. What is the WHO treatment regimen?
opts: Rifampicin 600 mg monthly + dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months
questions.exp: BI of 0 on SSS = paucibacillary (PB) leprosy. Well-formed epithelioid granulomas with Langhans cells indicate tuberculoid/borderline tuberculoid leprosy (PB spectrum). WHO-MDT for PB: rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised) + dapsone 100 mg daily (self-administered) for 6 months. Clofazimine is added in the MB regimen, which runs for 12 months.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with severe nocturnal pruritus involving the finger webs, wrists, and periumbilical area. Family members have similar complaints. Skin scraping reveals mites, eggs, and fecal pellets. What is the recommended treatment?
opts: Topical lindane 1% lotion applied once, washed after 8 hours
Permethrin 5% cream applied overnight and washed after 8-14 hours, repeated after 1 week
Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg single dose only
Topical sulfur 5% ointment for 1 night only
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is the first-line treatment for scabies: applied to the whole body from neck down, left on for 8-14 hours, and repeated after 1 week. It is safe in pregnancy and children >2 months. Lindane is effective but neurotoxic and contraindicated in pregnancy and infants. Oral ivermectin is used as an alternative or for crusted scabies. Sulfur ointment is safe in pregnancy but less effective than permethrin.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with digital ulcers, Raynaud's phenomenon, skin tightening over the hands and face, and dysphagia. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody is positive. What complication should be most actively screened for in this patient?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc). The most common and leading cause of death in anti-Scl-70 positive patients is interstitial lung disease (ILD). PAH is more strongly associated with anti-centromere antibodies (limited cutaneous SSc/CREST). Regular HRCT chest and pulmonary function tests (especially DLCO) are essential for ILD screening.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy with moderate acne has tried topical benzoyl peroxide with partial response. He is started on oral doxycycline. After 6 weeks of doxycycline, there is minimal improvement. What is the next most appropriate step?
opts: Perform comedone extraction and chemical peels
questions.exp: For moderate acne not responding to oral antibiotics + benzoyl peroxide, the next step is to add a topical retinoid (tretinoin) to address the comedonal component and enhance efficacy. Oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodulo-cystic acne, scarring acne, or failure of adequate courses of combination therapy (typically ≥6 months). Oral contraceptives are adjunctive in females. Comedone extraction is adjunctive only.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging red plaque on the lower leg with sharply demarcated, raised, advancing borders, warmth, tenderness, and fever. Which histological plane of the skin is primarily involved?
opts: Superficial dermis and upper dermis (with superficial lymphatics)
questions.exp: Erysipelas is a superficial skin infection involving the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep). The sharply demarcated, raised, bright red border reflects the superficial plane of involvement. Cellulitis involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and has less defined borders. Erysipelas's superficial location explains the sharp demarcation from surrounding normal skin.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters that rupture easily leaving raw erosions on the trunk, face, and oral mucosa. Nikolsky sign is positive. Tzanck smear shows acantholytic cells. ELISA confirms elevated antibodies against desmoglein 3. What is the target antigen in this condition?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (Dsg3), a desmosomal cadherin critical for keratinocyte adhesion in the suprabasal epidermis and mucosa. Mucosal involvement in PV correlates with anti-Dsg3. Anti-Dsg1 is seen in pemphigus foliaceus (no mucosal involvement). BP180 (collagen XVII) is the target in bullous pemphigoid. Laminin-332 is targeted in mucous membrane pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with multiple hypopigmented macules on the back and chest with fine scaling when scratched (positive coup d'ongle sign). Wood's lamp examination reveals yellow-green fluorescence. KOH mount shows short hyphae and clusters of yeast cells. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur, a lipophilic yeast that is part of normal skin flora. KOH mount showing short hyphae and round yeast cells ('spaghetti and meatballs' / 'bananas and grapes') is pathognomonic. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence due to pityriacitrin produced by Malassezia. The coup d'ongle sign reveals fine branny scales unique to this condition.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with HIV (CD4 120 cells/µL) presents with nodular, violaceous lesions on the lower extremities, hard palate, and trunk. Biopsy reveals proliferating spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. What is the causative agent?
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) in HIV/AIDS is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8, also known as KSHV). It presents with violaceous, purplish-brown nodules/plaques on lower extremities, face, and oral mucosa. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, extravasated RBCs, and plasma cells. HPV-16 causes squamous cell carcinoma. EBV causes EBV-associated lymphoma. HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with intensely itchy eczematous patches on flexural areas (antecubital and popliteal fossae) since childhood. She has asthma and allergic rhinitis. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. Which barrier defect is most important in the pathogenesis?
opts: Decreased ceramide levels and filaggrin mutation
Deficiency of involucrin in the stratum granulosum
Overexpression of loricrin in the stratum corneum
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis has a primary barrier defect: loss-of-function mutations in filaggrin (FLG) gene and decreased ceramide levels. Filaggrin is essential for proper stratum corneum formation; its deficiency is the strongest single genetic risk factor for AD. Reduced ceramides increase transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and allergen penetration. This barrier disruption leads to Th2 skewing and elevated IgE.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with erythema, edema, and bullae over the face and sun-exposed areas following starting a new medication. She also has photo-onycholysis. Which medication is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Doxycycline is a classic cause of phototoxic drug reactions. It absorbs UV radiation and generates reactive oxygen species, causing direct cell damage on sun-exposed skin (not immune-mediated). Photo-onycholysis (separation of the nail plate from the nail bed due to phototoxicity) is a characteristic feature of doxycycline and tetracycline class drugs. Hydroxychloroquine can cause photoallergic reactions. Metronidazole and amlodipine are not photosensitizers.

questions.q: A 65-year-old chronic smoker presents with an enlarging ulcer with raised, everted, indurated edges on the lower lip. Biopsy reveals well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Which regional lymph node group should be examined first?
questions.exp: SCC of the lower lip drains primarily to submental lymph nodes, then to submandibular and jugular chain nodes. Submental nodes are the first echelon (sentinel) lymph nodes for the lower lip and floor of mouth. Preauricular nodes drain the lateral face, temple, and ear. For SCC of the lip, careful palpation and imaging of the submental and submandibular triangle is essential for staging.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with multiple café-au-lait macules (>6, each >1.5 cm), axillary freckling, and multiple soft flesh-colored pedunculated nodules on the trunk and extremities. Her father has similar lesions. What is the mode of inheritance?
questions.exp: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1, von Recklinghausen's disease) is characterized by ≥6 café-au-lait macules (CALMs), axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe's sign), neurofibromas, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), and optic gliomas. NF1 is caused by mutations in the NF1 gene (chromosome 17q11.2) encoding neurofibromin, a tumor suppressor, and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. 50% of cases are de novo mutations.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with patchy hair loss showing exclamation mark hairs at the periphery of smooth, non-scarring patches. Dermoscopy shows yellow dots, black dots, and broken hairs. Thyroid function tests are normal. What is the pathomechanism?
opts: Scarring alopecia due to dermal fibrosis
T-cell mediated autoimmune attack on hair follicles
Miniaturization of follicles due to androgenic hormones
questions.exp: Alopecia areata is a T-cell mediated autoimmune disease targeting the hair follicle, particularly the anagen bulb (immune privilege collapse). CD8+ T cells recognize follicular antigens and cause follicular damage. Exclamation mark hairs (proximal thinning) are pathognomonic. Yellow dots (empty follicles with sebum), black dots, and broken hairs are seen on dermoscopy. It is not scarring, not androgenic, and not fungal.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs patch testing on a 35-year-old nurse with chronic hand eczema. Patches are applied to the upper back and removed at 48 hours. A positive reaction is noted at 96 hours but not at 48 hours. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is being tested?
questions.exp: Patch testing detects Type IV (delayed-type hypersensitivity/DTH) reactions, the immunological basis of allergic contact dermatitis. Sensitized T lymphocytes recognize hapten-protein complexes and release cytokines causing inflammation 48-96 hours after exposure. Reading at both 48 h and 96 h is essential because some reactions (e.g., neomycin) peak at 96-120 hours. Type I is tested by skin prick test (immediate, 15-20 min).

questions.q: A 45-year-old HIV-negative man presents with painless, progressive ulcerating lesions on the genitalia with a 'beefy red', friable granulomatous base and no lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows Donovan bodies within macrophages. What is the correct treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
Azithromycin 1 g weekly for at least 3 weeks
Oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 7 days
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis presents as beefy-red, painless, progressive genital ulcers without lymphadenopathy. Pathognomonic Donovan bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions within mononuclear cells on Giemsa/Leishman stain. CDC recommends azithromycin 1 g orally once weekly (or 500 mg daily) for at least 3 weeks until lesions heal. Doxycycline is an alternative. Penicillin treats syphilis; ceftriaxone treats gonorrhea.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man with vitiligo on the hands and face is started on narrowband UVB phototherapy. Which wavelength does NB-UVB use?
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) uses a wavelength of 311-313 nm, the most therapeutic and least carcinogenic part of the UVB spectrum. It is the most effective non-targeted phototherapy for vitiligo and psoriasis. NB-UVB stimulates residual melanocyte migration and melanogenesis. Broadband UVB spans 290-320 nm. UVA (320-400 nm) is used in PUVA therapy. 254 nm is used for germicidal purposes and causes significant DNA damage.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with symmetric hyperpigmentation of the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip worsening in summer. She is on oral contraceptive pills. Wood's lamp examination enhances the pigmentation. What layer of skin is most commonly affected?
questions.exp: Melasma most commonly affects the epidermis (epidermal type, 55-65%), where excess melanin is deposited in the basal and suprabasal layers. Wood's lamp enhances epidermal pigmentation (appears darker) but does not enhance dermal pigmentation. Dermal type (10-15%) has melanophages in dermis and does not enhance on Wood's lamp. Mixed type (30%) is most common in darker skin types. OCP and UV exposure are key triggers.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with recurrent epistaxis, telangiectasias on the lips, tongue, and fingertips, and a family history of similar lesions. He has had multiple gastrointestinal bleeds. What is the most likely underlying gene mutation?
questions.exp: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent epistaxis, and AVMs (lung, liver, brain, GI tract). HHT1 is caused by mutations in ENG (endoglin, chromosome 9q34) and HHT2 by ACVRL1 (ALK-1). Endoglin is a TGF-β co-receptor on vascular endothelium. PTCH1 mutations cause basal cell nevus (Gorlin) syndrome.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing and erythematous skin predominantly on the inner thighs and flexural areas. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the DEJ. ELISA confirms antibodies against BP180 and BP230. Which cells are the key effectors in the pathogenesis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease where IgG autoantibodies against BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230 fix complement and attract eosinophils and neutrophils to the DEJ. CD4+ Th2 cells drive autoantibody production and eosinophil recruitment; eosinophils release proteases that cleave the hemidesmosome-lamina lucida junction, causing subepidermal blister formation. Nikolsky sign is negative (subepidermal, not intraepidermal).

questions.q: During a facial skin biopsy procedure, the surgeon plans the elliptical incision parallel to the relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLEs). What is the primary advantage of this orientation?
opts: Minimal scarring and better cosmetic outcome
questions.exp: Relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLEs, also called Langer's lines or wrinkle lines) run perpendicular to the underlying muscle fibers. Incisions placed parallel to RSTLEs experience less tension during wound healing because forces act along rather than across the wound edges. This results in minimal scarring, a fine linear scar, and better cosmetic outcomes. Incisions perpendicular to RSTLEs are under tension and produce wider, more noticeable scars. This principle is fundamental to dermatological surgery.
